claims.text: Small changes in the relative concentrations of heavy transition metals tune the electronic density of states at the Fermi level in the proposed HEA.
The density of states at the Fermi level controls electron–phonon coupling strength.
Electron–phonon coupling strength governs superconductivity in the proposed HEA.
The target material is stipulated to be a single-phase disordered solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
Increasing or decreasing tungsten or molybdenum content by a small fraction while retaining the HEA compositional constraint is the proposed intervention.
Holding processing and thermal conditions constant ensures that superconductivity changes are attributable solely to composition.
Heavy-transition-metal atoms mediate the relevant local density of states at the Fermi level.
Compositional disorder and subtle lattice distortions influence the local density of states.
Changing heavy-transition-metal concentration modifies the electronic density of states.
Changing heavy-transition-metal concentration modifies the local lattice environment.
Changes in the electronic density of states and local lattice environment alter electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling raises the superconducting critical temperature.
Enhanced coupling raises Tc by lowering electron scattering caused by compositional randomness.
Increasing heavy-element concentration will produce a resolvable change in Tc relative to the baseline.
Increasing heavy-element concentration may either increase or decrease Tc depending on its effect on electron–phonon coupling and the density of states.
Short-range order dominates behavior in previously studied Nb–Ta or strongly titanium-rich systems.
Lattice strain and local ordering may compete with the proposed density-of-states and electron–phonon-coupling effects.
Transport and magnetic-susceptibility measurements can be used to determine Tc in the controlled comparison.
Failure to observe both a Tc change and a corresponding density-of-states alteration is proposed to falsify the mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome allows either an increase or a decrease in Tc, so the falsification rule's reference to a change 'opposite to the predicted trend' is undefined.

The mechanism gives a directional expectation that enhanced coupling raises Tc, but the stated outcome does not predict whether increasing the heavy-element concentration enhances or weakens coupling and therefore provides no directional composition-to-Tc prediction.
